summary: A Roman state governed through magistrates, assemblies and a powerful Senate that acquired an extensive Mediterranean empire before civil wars transformed its government.
currency: Bronze, silver and gold coinages, with the denarius a major silver denomination in the later Republic.
rulers: Selected officeholder: Marcus Tullius Cicero, consul in 63 BCE. Republican authority was shared among magistrates and the Senate.
economy: Conquest brought land, wealth and enslaved people into an agrarian state; the distribution of imperial gains intensified social conflict.
military: Citizen armies and allied forces expanded Roman control; successful generals increasingly turned military power against domestic rivals.
contributions: Republican magistracies, assemblies, law and military roads became influential institutional and infrastructural precedents.
origin: Tradition dates the expulsion of Rome’s last king and establishment of the Republic to 509 BCE.
decline: Civil wars, concentrated military power and political violence culminated in Octavian’s supremacy and the Augustan settlement of 27 BCE.
periodNote: 509 BCE is the traditional foundation date. Rome already possessed an empire while its constitutional government remained republican.
